said_voted.caption: Posts are shown as written. A post is matched to a vote only when it names the bill number or the bill's official title. A post can mention a bill for many reasons.

37 years ago today at @UCA_ES in San Salvador, El Salvador, six Jesuit priests and their housekeeper and her daughter were murdered by the Salvadoran military in a cold-blooded massacre that shocked the world.

Fathers Ignacio Ellacuría, “Nacho” Martin-Baró, and Segundo Montes —who I knew and had worked with—as well as Juan Ramon Moreno, Joaquin López y López, and Amando López were murdered in the early morning hours.

As a Congressional aide to Joe Moakley, I was asked to help lead the investigation into what happened. We uncovered that the Salvadoran military ordered the murder of the priests. Why? To silence their advocacy for the poor and marginalized people whose lives were being destroyed by civil war. We also uncovered that nearly every member of the unit that was ordered to commit this horrific crime was trained in the United States with American taxpayer dollars.
On this anniversary, let us all recommit ourselves to the values they lived and died for: peace, justice, human rights, and the dignity of every human being. The best way we can honor their memory is not simply to remember how they died, but to carry forward the work they dedicated their lives to.

37 years ago today at @UCA_ES in San Salvador, El Salvador, six Jesuit priests and their housekeeper and her daughter were murdered by the Salvadoran military in a cold-blooded massacre that shocked the world.

Fathers Ignacio Ellacuría, “Nacho” Martin-Baró, and Segundo Montes —who I knew and had worked with—as well as Juan Ramon Moreno, Joaquin López y López, and Amando López were murdered in the early morning hours.

As a Congressional aide to Joe Moakley, I was asked to help lead the investigation into what happened. We uncovered that the Salvadoran military ordered the murder of the priests. Why? To silence their advocacy for the poor and marginalized people whose lives were being destroyed by civil war. We also uncovered that nearly every member of the unit that was ordered to commit this horrific crime was trained in the United States with American taxpayer dollars.
On this anniversary, let us all recommit ourselves to the values they lived and died for: peace, justice, human rights, and the dignity of every human being. The best way we can honor their memory is not simply to remember how they died, but to carry forward the work they dedicated their lives to.
